topic.title: How the first transistor, two gold contacts on a plastic wedge at Bell Labs, became the switch inside every chip

title: What Did the First Transistor Actually Look Like?
description:
What did the first transistor actually look like?
At Bell Labs in December 1947, John Bardeen and Walter Brattain pressed two gold contacts onto a piece of germanium. We build it in 3D, show how it amplifies, then dive into a modern graphics chip built from the same switch.
Sources: Computer History Museum, NVIDIA GeForce News (Sep 2022).
Animations are simplified illustrations, not exact to scale.
cta: Which invention should we rebuild next? Comment

lines.text: Every chip you own is built from a Bell Labs invention.
The transistor. What did the very first one look like?
In 1947, John Bardeen and Walter Brattain built it by hand.
Brattain wrapped gold foil around a plastic wedge and slit it at the tip with a razor.
Two gold contacts, almost touching, pressed by a spring onto germanium. So how does that do anything?
A small voltage on one contact controls the current through the other.
On December sixteenth, a weak signal came out up to 100 times stronger.
Why does it matter? The same trick is a switch: a small signal turns a big current on or off.
Shrink it, copy it, and one NVIDIA Ada Lovelace graphics chip holds up to 76B of them.
All from gold foil on a plastic wedge: the switch now inside every chip in your phone.

dive: 'one NVIDIA graphics chip holds up to 76B of them' is out of date. The 76B ceiling is NVIDIA's Sep 2022 figure for Ada Lovelace (confirmed on nvidia.com), but newer NVIDIA chips are bigger: the RTX 5090's GB202 has about 92.2B (PC Gamer, hwcooling) and data-centre Blackwell dies have more. Stated today, 'up to 76B' is wrong. Fix: tie it to its chip and year, e.g. 'one NVIDIA graphics chip from 2022 holds up to 76B of them', or re-source a current count.

flow: 'A tiny current into one contact lets a far bigger one through the other' misstates how the point-contact transistor worked. The source (CHM) says 'the voltage on one contact modulated the current flowing through the other'. Its current gain was small (about 1 to 3); the 100x gain was in signal strength, not one current against the other. Expert viewers will catch it (profile: accuracy over spectacle). Fix: e.g. 'A small voltage on one contact controls the current through the other.' Redraw the flow visuals (thin cyan trickle vs thick amber stream) to match.
